title: Global Negation Strategies: A Comparative Analysis
description: An  investigation into the distribution of negation strategies using Grambank and WALS datasets.
contents:

Section 1: Grambank Areal and Genealogical Distribution
The following analysis examines whether negation strategies are primarily driven by geographic proximity (areal diffusion) or family lineage (genealogical inheritance). I focus on two key features GB107 (affixal/clitic negation) and GB137 (clause-final negation).
1.1 Chi-Squared Tests for Areal Effect
In order to evaluate the areal diffusion, I utilised Pearson’s Chi-squared tests. These tests enable me to determine whether the presence of a negation strategy is significantly associated with specific geographic macroareas.

1.3 Feature Co-occurrence and Correlation
While the previous section focus on the external drivers of negation of geography and ancestry, it is also critical to examine the internal relationship in between these markers. This section investigates whether the use of affixal negation (GB107) and clause-final negation (GB137) are independent structural choices or if they exhibit a significant typological correlation.
The following Chi-squared test evaluates this dependency. A significant result would suggest that the presence of one negation strategy may historically or structurally constrain the development of the other, thus suggesting a deeper cross-linguistic pattern in how negation is encoded.

1.4 Visualising Regional Variation
While Chi-squared tests provide statistical evidence for areal and genealogical trends, visualising these distributions may reveal a potential geographical ‘shape’ of negation. In this section I contrast clause-final negation (GB137) with affixal negation (GB107) and through plotting these as proportional bar charts across macroareas, it may be possible to determine if certain regions favour specific structural blueprints for negation.



The resulting visualisations highlight a clear divergence in how these two strategies are distributed globally. Clause-final negation exhibits significant peaks in specific macroareas like South America and Papuanesia, perhaps suggesting that this syntactic features may spread through language contact. However, affixal negation shows a more balanced, presence across most macroareas. This suggests that morphological negation is often a deeply embedded trait that is less prone to being lost or gained through geographical proximity and therefore more likely to be inherited vertically through language families.

The above Chi-squared results for the WALS data 113A and 143G reveals no statistically significant correlations. Unlike the regional clustering observed in the Grambank data, these results suggest that the choice between symmetric and asymmetric negation strategies is not strictly dictated by basic word orders or the position of the negative element.
The independence may indicate that these structural dimensions evolve through different typological pressures. As while a language may shift its negative position due to contact or changes in word-order, the internal symmetry of its negation system appears to remain as a distinct and independent structural trait.
2.2 Visualising Proportional Trends
While the previous Chi-squared test confirms a lack of statistical correlation, the following proportional plot allows for the inspection of how clausal symmetry (113A) is distributed across different syntactic positions (143G). Through this standardisation of frequencies to 100%, the relative prevalence of symmetric versus asymmetric negation strategies for both V-Neg and Neg-V word orders become observable.
The resulting distribution illustrates the structural diversity of negation, as it demonstrates that neither syntactic position (113A or 143G) constrains a language into a specific morphological pathway. Noticeably, however, the data does reveal that symmetric strategies are only present within the Neg-V category, therefore potentially suggesting that these features are generally governed by independent evolutionary typological pressures, despite certain morphological configurations that may be restricted to specific word-order environments.



Section 3: Comparing WALS and Grambank Datasets
To synthesize the previous findings, I plotted the global distributions of WALS 113A (Clausal symmetry), alongside Grambank GB137 (Clause-final negation). Mapping these features allows me to move beyond abstract percentages and observe the actual geographic densities of negation strategies. These comparison visualisations highlight how specific structural choices cluster in particular regions, thus providing a final layer of evidence for the areal and genealogical trends discussed throughout this analysis.



The comparison between the WALS and Grambank maps illustrates the complementary nature of each dataset. While the WALS map (above) captures a broad typological overview of clausal symmetry with a focus on categorical variety, the Grambank map (below) provides a more dense, binary snapshot of syntactic positioning. In combination, they reveal that certain regions are hot-spots for diverse negation strategies. These maps confirm that while negation is a universal linguistic requirement, its structural implementation is deeply tied to the geographic and historical context of the world’s language families.

Overview
In this assignment, I will work with a simulated A/B test run by a fictitious political party delivering messages on its official website.
The party wants to increase the probability that visitors sign up as supporters.
To do this, they are going to test two homepage versions:
Control homepage (Version A):
Standard party messaging (policy highlights, leader photo, “Join us” button).
Issue-focused homepage (Version B):
Emphasizes a hot-button issue, such as immigration, important to the party’s base, plus a “Join us” button.
Visitors are randomly assigned to Version A or Version B when they land on the website.
The outcome variable is:
support_signup = 1 if the website visitor signs up as a party-supporter
support_signup = 0 otherwise

Written Analysis
What does treatment represent in this experiment?
Within the above experiment, ‘treatment’ refers to the random assignment of web traffic to two different political website homepages. A given value of 0 indicates the visitor saw the control page, while an individual with a value of 1 viewed a homepage that focused on a relevant hot-topic.
What are Y0 and Y1, conceptually?
Y0 and Y1 represent potential outcomes. Y0 depicts the signup decision a visitor may have made having viewed the standard homepage. However, Y1 is the decision that the same visitor may have made upon viewing the issue-focused webpage. 
Why do we only observe one of Y0 or Y1 for each visitor? Why is this a problem for causality?
Each visitor can only produce either Y0 or Y1 as they are only shown the assigned website homepage once. This is due to the problem of causal inference. As both outcomes cannot be viewed by a single individual, the individual treatments effects cannot be measured and causality is determined through averaging the outcomes of each group.
What does support_signup represent in terms of potential and realised outcomes?
‘support_signup’ represents the realised outcome, which is shown as a visitor’s ‘yes’ or ‘no’ decision. This contrasts from the Y1 and Y0, as these represent the possible decisions a visitor may make whereas ‘support_signup’ is the actual result received from an individual that is recorded along with their assigned website homepage

Assuming I was hired as an analyst for the political party and I have to present these findings to my employer. The people that I am giving the presentation to do not have much quantitative experience. How might I show the information above in a way that is easy to understand?:
How different are the predicted sign-up probabilities from the two models for each group?
Within the control group both models indicated a potential signup rate of ~11.85%. The treatment group models suggest a signup rate of ~16.02%. Thus whether utilising a linear or logit model, it was found that the treatment increased the chance of an individual signing up by ~4.17% 
Does either model seem clearly inappropriate here, or do they both tell a similar story?
Although using a linear model in many complex scenarios may be considered inappropriate due to the potential output of impossible probabilities, i.e. -5% or 115%. Within A/B testing, both the linear and logit models are considered ‘saturated’. This means that they identify the averages across a specified group and therefore, as seen in the above plot, the outcomes are the same.
Which model is preferable and why?
In the context of presenting this information to individuals who may lack a complex understanding of quantitative methods, the preferred method would be the linear model. This model allows for an easier interpretation of the 4.17% increase as log-odds do not need to be explained. Therefore increasing clarity for more intuitive decision-making as well as saving time and effort.

Ethical Reflection on Political A/B Testing
So far, I have treated this like a standard A/B test. But here the product is a political message, and the outcome is political support.
What could be some potential ethical considerations that may arise when a political party runs an A/B test on website visotors?
Through conducting A/B testing, in the eyes of analysts, the voters are transformed into data points which raises some significant ethical concerns in terms of informed consent. Unlike with usual methods and fields of research, conducting experiments through the use of political messaging can create a direct impact on civic beliefs and election outcomes. The use of statistical models that isolate ‘high interest’ voters may enable political parties to micro-target specific groups of individuals, perhaps causing filter bubbles in which differing target groups receive alternate contradictory promises. Furthermore, utilising this practice may deteriorate shared factual political realities through a prioritisation of persuasion over public interaction.
In addition, although Average Treatment Effect (ATE) can measure mathematical efficiency, it does not account for the contents of an imposed treatment condition. For example, using a 4.17% lift as a method of justification for fear-based messaging or misinformation underscores an intense conflict between statistical successes and real-world moral responsibilities. As website traffic would likely be unaware of their participation in online behavioural experiments, this treatment condition may end up shifting an individual’s political supports and thus the lack of transparency may adjust just persuasion toward psychological engineering.
In consequence, there is a risk of immorality within political parties that incorporate unwitting internet traffic into research may prioritise percentage lift over the necessity of informed consent and participation. An approach such as this may be viewed as conversion-focused and thus may reduce democratic transparency to data-driven transactions, perhaps erosion the transparency of which public trust is built upon.
